blocks.text: This itself is plainly false, and rests on a strange error of our author, by which, in the passages which he will presently adduce from Arabic writers, he reads حمص [ḥimmaṣ] chickpea instead of حمض [ḥamḍ], i.e. saline herbs. This observation is owed to Ol. Celsius, who in Hierobot. vol. II, p. 234, treating the קלי of the Hebrews, says the following: "Bochart labours most learnedly, as is his habit, to make Kali in 2 Sam. XVII, 28. into chickpea. But, deceived either by less correct manuscripts of the Arabs or by something else, he consistently reads حمص [ḥimmaṣ] chickpea instead of حمض [ḥamḍ] in the Arabs whom he cites, and confuses different things. This I make clear from my Abu'l-Fadl. Under the heading اشنان [ushnān] he says this: اشنان معروف ويسمي الحرض وهو من الحمض وهو كل نابت فيه ملوحة [ushnān maʿrūf wa-yusmī al-ḥurḍ wa-huwa min al-ḥamḍ wa-huwa kull nābit fīhi mulūḥa] Usnen is well known, and is called Alhord, and it belongs to الحمض [al-ḥamḍ], the name by which all herbs are called in which there is saltiness. The verb itself is in Golius, Lex. Arab. p. 653: حمض [ḥamaḍa] the camel grazed on the bitter and salty plant which is called حمض [ḥamḍ]. And in the 4th conjugation: the land abounded in salty and bitter plants." Thus Celsius, and his words are confirmed by the matter itself. For since all the writers whom Bochart brings forward unanimously attribute a saline taste to the plants Usnen and Alkali, it is self-evident that these are to be classed not among chickpeas, حمص [ḥimmaṣ], but among saline herbs, حمض [ḥamḍ]. Nor am I moved by the fact that حمص [ḥimmaṣ] is read here instead of حمض [ḥamḍ] not in just one passage of a single writer, but consistently in absolutely all the passages that our author adduces from various authors. For when Bochart found, no doubt through a copyist's carelessness, حمص [ḥimmaṣ] written instead of حمض [ḥamḍ] in one of these writers, he eagerly seized upon the chickpea in favour of his preconceived opinion, and inserted it into the other passages too which he cites from other writers, silently putting حمص [ḥimmaṣ] in them instead of حمض [ḥamḍ]. That Bochart did not act faithfully enough here is certainly shown by what will be observed in the following note. Therefore in what follows, حمص [ḥimmaṣ], chickpea, must always be replaced by حمض [ḥamḍ], saline plants, except for the last passage of Ibn al-Baytar on قاقلي [qāqulī],
Rather, what is read there is: a species of saline plant, similar to اشنان [ushnān].

This would truly be so, if قلي [qilī] belonged to the حمض [ḥimmaṣ]—that is, the chickpeas. As it is, since it is among the saline herbs (حمض [ḥamḍ]), it can have nothing in common with the Hebrew קלי, which Celsius, Hierobot. vol. II, p. 231 ff., shows is rightly explained as roasted grain.
This argument, since it rests on the opinion that Usnen and Kali are a species of chickpea (حمص [ḥimmaṣ]), collapses completely once that opinion is removed (by what we observed in note 5).

It hardly seems necessary to warn the reader that all this has been argued in vain, since the thing which the Arabs call dove's dung is not of the chickpea kind (on which, as on a foundation, Bochart's whole argument rests), but a species of saline plant, as we have amply proved in note 5. Of lesser weight is what Otho Verbrugge said in support of Bochart's opinion in Observatt. Philologg. de nominum Hebraeorum plurali numero, Groningen 1730, in duodecimo, p. 7–8. He himself thinks that חרייונים means small loaves, from a singular חרייון, which he takes to be a diminutive of חרי, a kind of bread among the Chaldeans and Talmudists. This opinion will hardly win anyone's approval, since what is said of the חרייונים in the sacred text, that they were measured by kabs, in no way suits loaves. Much more absurd is what Hiller put forward in Hierophyt. vol. II, ch. 22, sect. 3, p. 129: that חריינים are dove's holes, that is, the entrails of doves, which, being perforated, draw nourishment and growth out of the body. All these things weighed, it is best to retain that interpretation of this much-vexed word which Bochart listed in first place at the beginning of this chapter, but rejected there; yet undeservedly, as we have shown in note 1.
